text: Hi, how's it going? I'm a big coffee lover, so I guess I'll start there. I can't really start my day without a cup of coffee, and this morning was no different. I had one before I came to take this test, and I'm already looking forward to another one once it's over. I work in IT, and my days are pretty busy. I live in an apartment, and I'm pretty much a homebody. In my free time, I like listening to music, playing computer games, and reading. So, yeah, that's me in a nutshell: coffee, music, and my computer. I'm happy to be here, and I hope I do well today!

Well, I'm kind of into K-pop these days, and I have a favorite group. To be honest, I never thought I'd say that at my age. It all started in the car. A friend of mine kept playing their songs on the way to the mall, and I pretended I hated it. But after a few weeks, I caught myself humming along! The songs are catchy, the dance moves are sharp, and the singers really seem to enjoy themselves. Now I have their whole playlist on my phone. My friend laughs at me and says, "You're a fan now." She's right. Funny how a friend can change your taste in music.

I listen to music pretty much all day long. In the morning, I drive along the coast to work, and that's my favorite time. I turn up the volume and sing along with my coffee in the cup holder. At work, I put on headphones when I'm fixing a server problem. It helps me focus. At home, I listen in my room after dinner. I don't really listen to the radio anymore. I just use a music app, because I can pick whatever I want. But I do go to concerts, once in a blue moon. Last year, a friend and I went to a K-pop concert. I was the oldest guy there by far! But when the lights went off and everybody waved their light sticks, I got goosebumps. Live music is just different.

I got into music because of my family. We had a little cassette player, and it was always on, playing sad ballads from the radio. I didn't get a vote! So I grew up humming those songs without even knowing it. In my teens, I started buying my own tapes, and I was into rock and pop from overseas. I loved guitar solos. Then in my twenties and thirties, I mostly listened to calm music while I worked. These days, I'm back to pop, thanks to my friends. So, I guess my taste has gone full circle. I started with those old ballads, and now I'm learning K-pop dances from my friends. Well, trying to, anyway!

Korea has really great public transportation. In Seoul, the subway goes almost everywhere, and you can transfer to a bus for almost nothing. You just tap your card. For long trips, there's the KTX, our high-speed train. You can go from Seoul to Busan in about two and a half hours. Taxis are cheap and easy to catch, and you can call one on your phone. Of course, a lot of people drive too. In smaller cities, it's a little different. Most people have a car, and in some places, ferries go out to the small islands. I'd say Korea is one of the most convenient countries to get around in.

I drive almost everywhere. Living in my city, I really can't get by without a car. I drive to work every morning, and it takes about 20 minutes. I love my commute, because I drive along the sea, and it's like a mini vacation. I usually take my coffee and music with me. On weekends, I drive my family to the mall or to visit relatives. Honestly, the only time I take public transportation is when I go to Seoul. Then I take the KTX, and I get on the subway. I like it, because I can sit back and play a game on my phone. But in my city, my car is my second home.

When I was a kid, we didn't have a car. Back then, most families didn't. So we walked everywhere. I walked to school with my friends, and it took about 30 minutes. In the winter, my nose would freeze. When we had to go far, we took the bus. It was always packed, and I was so small that I'd get squished in the middle. I also had a bicycle. It was a hand-me-down from a cousin, so it was kind of pink! I rode it around the village anyway, because I didn't care. Honestly, I was just happy to have wheels. People got around slowly back then, but I miss it. It felt like we had more time to talk.

One city I really enjoyed was Taipei, in Taiwan. We went with my family. It's close to Korea, so it was an easy trip. The city was lively but laid-back. There were night markets everywhere, and the smell of street food was in the air. We tried stinky tofu, which I thought I'd hate, but it was surprisingly good! We also had bubble tea almost every day. What I loved most was the people. They were so friendly and helpful. One time we looked lost, and a stranger walked up and asked, "Can I help you?" In English, too! I felt really welcome. It's the kind of place you want to go back to.

My first trip abroad was to Osaka, in Japan, with a friend. It was a long time ago. I'd never been on a plane before, so I was a nervous wreck. When the plane took off, I held on to my seat and my friend just laughed at me. But once we got there, I forgot all about it. We ate our way through the city: takoyaki, ramen, and grilled meat. We walked around Dotonbori at night, and the neon lights were amazing. I remember thinking, "Wow, the world is so big." We only stayed four days, but it was the start of my love for traveling. To this day, I still remember the taste of that first takoyaki.

Yes, I have. It happened in Taipei. One afternoon, we were walking around when it suddenly started pouring. I mean, it was like someone turned on a shower! We had no umbrellas, and we got soaked in about 30 seconds. We ran into the first little noodle shop we saw. It was a tiny place with just five tables. The owner took one look at us, and handed us some towels. Then, without us asking, she brought us four bowls of hot beef noodle soup. She said, "On the house!" We stayed for two hours, waiting for the rain to stop, and the owner chatted with us with a mix of Chinese and English. It turned out to be the best meal of the trip. We didn't even plan it! What made it memorable was her kindness. I think of it every time it rains.

Hi, my car broke down a few blocks away. I think I need some help. I was driving, and it suddenly made a strange noise and stopped. I have a few questions. First, can you take a look at it right now?. Okay. Do you know what might be wrong with it?. I see. How long will the repair take?. And roughly how much will it cost?. Got it. One last thing: is there a place nearby where I can wait, or can you give me a ride?. Great. Do you take credit cards?. Thanks so much. You're a lifesaver!

Hello, I'm so sorry, but I have some bad news. I'm not going to make it to our meeting on time. My car broke down on the way, and I'm stuck at a repair shop in a small town. I feel terrible, because I know how important this meeting is. But I have a few ideas. First, how about we do the meeting by video call? I can join from the shop, as soon as I get a Wi-Fi connection. Or if that's not good, we can push the meeting back to this afternoon, or even to tomorrow morning. And if you're in a hurry, I can send my colleague to go over the details with you. What works best for you? Again, I'm really sorry for the trouble. I'll make it up to you.

Let me think. Oh, I remember one cold winter morning. I had a big meeting at work, so I left home early. I got in the car, turned the key, and nothing. Not even a click. I tried again, and the same thing. I had a bad feeling. Then I looked up and saw the dome light was on. I'd left it on all night! The battery was totally dead. I felt so stupid. It was freezing, and I was already running late. So I called a coworker who lived nearby, and he came over with jumper cables. He gave my car a jump start, and it worked. I made it to the meeting just in time, though I was a bit out of breath. After that, I bought my own jumper cables, and now I always check the lights. And I owe that coworker a coffee, by the way!

Coffee shops have changed a lot over the years. Back in the day, people went there just to drink coffee and meet someone. It was a place for dates and business talks. But these days, it's totally different. People go to cafes to study, work on their laptops, or just hang out. We even have a word for it: "cafe study". I see students sitting there for hours with one cup of coffee! People also go for the dessert, the cool interior, and to take pictures for social media. Some cafes are more like art galleries. Honestly, for a lot of people, the coffee is just an excuse. They're really paying for the space, a place to relax and be by themselves.

I think coffee shops are popular because they're affordable and easy. For the price of a cup of coffee, you get a comfy seat, free Wi-Fi, and a break from the busy world. They're a kind of "third place", somewhere between home and work. At home, I get distracted. At the office, I'm always on call. But in a cafe, I can finally breathe. In my city, we have so many cafes with ocean views. My friend and I sometimes sit by the window with two lattes and watch the ships go by. We don't even have to talk. For me, a cafe is a small daily reset. So, coffee shops play a big role in people's lives. They're where we meet, think, and recharge.
